title: Future of Professionals Report 2025: Strategic AI Adoption — Unlocking Innovation and Maximizing Returns
pub: Thomson Reuters Institute (third annual Future of Professionals report)
author: Thomson Reuters Institute

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The report accepts the cluster’s core proposition that AI should be deployed selectively within human-led workflows and that value depends on verification, user capability and operating-model redesign. It materially extends the synthesis with a four-layer implementation framework and survey-based associations between visible strategy, operational change and reported ROI, while its productivity and competitive-gap claims remain forecasts or non-causal associations.
qs: Operational — Although it may look different for different types of organizations, those that are making changes to how they deliver their work in terms of resourcing and pricing models, adapting                                                                                     Operations workflow and processes, and adding new roles and skills to support will see more success.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s emphasis on workflow reconfiguration, organizational complements and user capability rather than tool access alone. Its survey evidence links strategic, process-level adoption to stronger reported returns and identifies training, AI proficiency and change-supporting culture as necessary foundations. It also records emerging reductions in junior intake and role redesign, consistent with competence and workforce risks, though it does not directly examine verification or apprenticeship effects.

st.t: Operating model: AI shifts bargaining across providers
st.an: The report supports the cluster’s view that AI advantage depends on strategic process redesign and deliberate redeployment of productivity gains, rather than tool adoption alone. Its quantified benefits are forecasts based on surveyed expectations, consistent with the cluster’s caution that broad returns are not yet demonstrated.

st.t: Task transformation: Staff reductions coexist with development
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s cautious framing by treating AI as a persistent concern alongside economic, geopolitical and demographic pressures, while reporting increased concern about skilled-labour shortages. It does not present evidence of AI-driven mass displacement, automation-related staff reductions, or the effectiveness of workforce development measures.

st.t: Work redesign: Organisation captures more value than access
st.an: The source directly supports the proposition that AI advantage depends more on coordinated organisational strategy, infrastructure and workflow integration than on tool adoption or isolated task efficiencies. Its revenue-growth claim is associative rather than causal, and its acceptance of deliberately measured adoption adds nuance without weakening that position.

kp.k: Survey spans legal and other professional services
kp.d: The report draws on 2,275 survey responses collected in February and March 2025 across legal, risk, compliance, tax, accounting, audit and trade professionals, including outside firms and in-house functions. The sample includes 1,363 legal respondents and 257 corporate C-Suite respondents. Findings presented for professionals generally should be distinguished from the report’s specifically legal findings.
qs: Our third annual Future of Professionals report draws on comprehensive research across multiple sectors

kp.k: Expected transformation exceeds immediate organizational change
kp.d: Eighty percent of respondents expect AI to have a high or transformational impact on their profession within five years, while 38% expect high or transformational organizational change in 2025. Thirty percent believe their organization is moving too slowly in adoption. These are respondent expectations and perceptions rather than demonstrated future outcomes.
qs: Disconnect between future aspiration and current pace
Are professionals on track to realize the future they envisioned?

kp.k: Respondents report benefits beyond time savings
kp.d: Fifty-three percent report their organizations already seeing ROI directly or indirectly associated with AI investment. The report describes efficiency, productivity, faster responses and fewer errors as common benefits, with more advanced organizations pursuing quality improvements, financial gains, work-life balance, skills development and recruitment or retention benefits. Its ROI category encompasses these varied reported benefits.
qs: More than half of organizations are already seeing ROI because of AI adoption

kp.k: Visible strategies correlate with greater reported returns
kp.d: The report classifies 31% as having no significant organizational AI adoption plans, 43% as adopting without a strategy and 22% as having a visible strategy; respectively, 23%, 64% and 81% report ROI. It reports a 3.5-times association between visible strategies and experiencing at least one form of ROI compared with no significant plans, and a 1.9-times association with revenue growth compared with informal adoption. In-house departments with their own strategies also report more ROI than departments without strategies or following only an organization-wide strategy.
qs: Layer 1: Having a clear AI strategy is strongest lever for success
Those with a visible AI strategy are 3.5x as likely to be experiencing at least one form of ROI
compared to those without any significant plans for AI adoption.

kp.k: Leadership and governance support strategic implementation
kp.d: The report recommends four implementation layers: strategy, leadership, operations and individual users. Professionals whose leaders lead by example are reported as 1.7-times as likely to experience AI benefits; active technology investment is associated with 2.0-times the likelihood, and adding governance roles with 1.5-times. Fifteen percent of law and tax/audit firms added leadership or governance roles in the previous year. Suggested governance changes include moving beyond lawyer-only executive committees to incorporate operations and transformation leadership. These reported associations support the report’s recommendations, rather than establishing causal effects.
qs: Layer 2: Strong leaders lead by example in times of change

kp.k: Operations change across roles, workflows and service offerings
kp.d: The report recommends adapting staffing, workflows, services, delivery models and pricing, and says organizations making such changes report more ROI. Around a quarter to a third have recruited new roles, appointed consultants or increased existing roles. Only around one in ten have begun decreasing existing types of roles, including junior intake, relocating roles to lower-cost geographies or redefining roles. Twenty-six percent of firms introduced advisory or consultancy services in the preceding 12 months; 30% of in-house corporate and government professionals began purchasing them. Thirteen percent of firms offer AI-powered services, while 23% of in-house professionals report purchasing them. These figures concern the report’s broader professional-services population, not law firms alone.
qs: Layer 3: Adjusting operations can gain the most benefits from AI

kp.k: Pricing flexibility affects in-house purchasing decisions
kp.d: A third of firms are increasing the proportion of work billed other than hourly. A quarter of in-house professionals increased work with firms because of offered fee arrangements, and a similar proportion dropped a firm for insufficient fee flexibility. One-fifth of in-house departments significantly changed the proportion of work performed internally, with slightly fewer changing outsourced allocation. The report treats these as operational adjustments relevant to realizing AI benefits, rather than documenting wholesale replacement of hourly billing.

kp.k: Adoption remains uneven across organizations and individuals
kp.d: Forty-six percent report organizational investment in new AI-powered technologies in the previous 12 months, but only 30% regularly use AI to start tasks or edit drafted text. The report interprets low investment combined with high individual usage as a public-tool safeguard risk, and high investment with low usage as poor change management and wasted investment. Corporate legal departments show relatively high investment and usage, whereas government agencies are low on both. It reports that Millennials adopt AI at nearly twice the rate of Baby Boomers.
qs: Organizations follow different paths toward AI adoption
Individual adoption rates also vary by demographic:

kp.k: Individual adoption goals often lack strategic alignment
kp.d: Although 96% have at least basic awareness of AI capabilities and 81% have tried AI, 71% lack a good understanding of practical applications and 70% are not regular users. Thirty-nine percent have personal AI adoption goals. Among respondents with personal goals, 65% are unaware of an organizational strategy; conversely, 38% with an organizational strategy lack personal goals. The report warns that these mismatches threaten consistent implementation, accountability and efficiency.

kp.k: Accuracy concerns sustain demand for human verification
kp.d: Reported investment barriers include demonstrable accuracy (50%), budget (45%), data security (42%), ethical concerns (37%) and implementation time or resources (36%). Ninety-one percent believe computers should face higher accuracy standards than humans; 41% require AI output to be 100% accurate before use without human review. The report consequently emphasizes continuing human review. These figures measure respondents’ standards and concerns, not actual model accuracy.
qs: still critical that humans continue to review

kp.d: Overreliance on technology at the expense of professional skill development is the leading reported negative consequence of concern, at 24%, ahead of privacy, confidentiality and transparency (15%), malicious uses (14%), data security implications (13%) and widespread job loss (9%). The report interprets this as a shift from early fears of displacement toward concern that successful AI use could weaken professional development.

kp.k: Modern professionals augment rather than abandon core abilities
kp.d: The report’s competence framework retains technical expertise, research and writing, critical and strategic thinking, interpersonal effectiveness, and organizational skills, with AI augmenting each. Illustrative legal tasks include analyzing case-law patterns, predicting judicial outcomes, drafting documents and contracts, and summarizing technical material; these are examples, not measured performance results. Fifty-five percent report significant day-to-day role changes in the previous year or expect them in the next year, and 88% favor a profession-specific AI assistant. Respondents differ on whether assistants will become standard competitive equipment, a differentiator or simply a benefit.

kp.k: Broad, active learning supports AI proficiency
kp.d: Forty-six percent report team skills gaps, with 31% reporting technology and data gaps and 10% technical-domain gaps. Learning activities include reading (87%), experimentation (77%), informal peer learning (76%), virtual training (72%), in-person training (54%) and online courses (50%). The report associates varied learning methods and active training with stronger proficiency. Those involved in organizational AI development are most proficient, but it explicitly allows that technology-interested professionals may self-select into involvement. Gen Z respondents are twice as likely as Baby Boomers to identify colleagues’ insufficient digital literacy; Gen X participates in AI training at higher rates than younger colleagues.
qs: Addressing the skills gap among modern professionals
How professionals have been learning about the latest forms of AI
active training, both in-person and online.

kp.k: Workforce redesign includes technology and business roles
kp.d: The report identifies recruitment by law and tax/accounting firms in technology and AI, specialist professional work, operations, innovation and transformation, business development and marketing, and client experience. Corporate and government teams recruit in technology and AI, risk and compliance, sustainability/ESG, operations, and innovation and transformation. It recommends establishing new roles and rethinking existing ones to attract versatile, technology-capable professionals, without offering a quantified forecast of legal staffing leverage or partner-associate structures.

kp.k: Time savings and competitive disruption remain prospective
kp.d: The foreword says surveyed legal professionals expect nearly 240 hours freed annually, up from 200 in 2024, based on the predicted adoption pace. It assigns this an average annual value of $19,000 per professional and a $32 billion combined US legal and tax/accounting impact. These are anticipated savings and valuations, not demonstrated realized totals. In its commentary, Thomson Reuters predicts that organizations reinventing processes will outperform slower adopters and warns that failing to develop an AI strategy in 2025 risks falling behind within three years, potentially placing almost one-third of organizations on a path to failure. It nevertheless accepts deliberately measured adoption when aligned with organizational goals and recommends faster integration for standardized tasks than for work requiring nuanced judgment.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Thomson Reuters Institute presents AI as an augmenting technology whose benefits and competitive effects depend on strategic adoption, operational redesign and individual proficiency.
pts.d: The report says 80% of surveyed professionals expect AI to have a high or transformational impact within five years, while 53% report their organizations already experience at least one benefit or form of ROI. Reported benefits include efficiency, productivity, faster responses, fewer errors, cost reductions, revenue growth and talent-related improvements. In his foreword, Thomson Reuters CEO Steve Hasker says surveyed legal professionals expect nearly 240 hours of annual time savings, versus 200 in 2024, assigning an average annual value of $19,000 per professional and a combined US annual impact of $32 billion across legal and tax/accounting. These are anticipated savings and valuations, not reported measurements of realized legal-sector output. The Institute reports that visible-strategy organizations experience at least one form of ROI at a rate of 81%, compared with 64% for informal adopters and 23% for organizations without significant adoption plans; strategic adopters are 1.9 times as likely as informal adopters to report AI-related revenue growth. Its commentary predicts that firms redesigning processes and reinvesting productivity gains will outperform slower competitors, and warns that organizations failing to develop a strategy in 2025 risk falling behind within three years. Hasker frames professional displacement as competition from AI-enabled peers rather than direct replacement by AI. The report describes AI-assisted research, drafting, summarization, regulatory analysis and workflow management as augmentation of continuing core professional abilities. It also identifies overreliance and impaired skill development as concerns and argues that human review remains critical.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is a February–March 2025 cross-professional survey; competitive forecasts and recommendations are the Institute’s and Hasker’s interpretations of that evidence.
pts.d: The third annual report draws on 2,275 responses across legal, tax, accounting, audit, trade, risk and compliance, plus corporate C-suite respondents. There are 1,363 legal respondents: 985 in firms, 197 in business/corporations and 191 in government. The sample includes 1,021 US respondents and respondents in nine other regional categories. Most headline percentages concern the combined professional sample rather than lawyers alone. The report supplies survey associations between reported benefits and visible strategy, investment, governance changes, leadership behavior, knowledge, regular use and personal adoption goals. For example, respondents describing leaders as leading by example are 1.7 times as likely to report benefits, and regular AI users are 2.4 times as likely as nonregular users to report organizational benefits. The material provides no controlled causal study establishing that these factors produce the differences. It treats ROI broadly, including nonfinancial benefits, rather than supplying audited investment-return calculations. Time savings are expectations, and the supplied text does not explain the calculation behind the dollar valuations. Concerns and accuracy thresholds are respondent opinions: 24% identify overreliance at the expense of skill development as their principal negative consequence, 50% identify demonstrable accuracy as an investment barrier, 91% want computers held to higher accuracy standards than humans, and 41% require complete accuracy before dispensing with human review. The Institute explicitly allows for selection effects in its association between involvement in AI development and proficiency. Predictions of competitive failure and career disadvantage are interpretive forecasts, not observed future outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The report distinguishes current reported adoption and benefits from annual savings expectations and forecasts extending one to five years.
pts.d: The evidence reflects responses collected in February and March 2025. Investment and many operational-change questions concern the preceding 12 months; anticipated changes often concern the following 12 months. Although 80% foresee high or transformational professional impact within five years, only 38% expect such organizational change in 2025. Hasker predicts transformation across the covered professions over three years. The Institute warns that not developing an AI strategy in 2025 risks competitive disadvantage within three years, while operational redesign is expected to unfold iteratively over several years. Annual time-savings projections depend on the predicted pace of adoption. Benefits are conditional on alignment with organizational goals, visible strategy, leadership participation, workflow and pricing changes, individual learning, regular use and accountability. The report does not prescribe equally rapid adoption everywhere: standardized, repeatable tasks are presented as suitable for faster integration, whereas nuanced judgment and nonstandard analysis warrant a more measured approach. It recognizes a deliberately measured but goal-aligned adoption strategy as valid. It warns that investment without use can be wasted and that individual use without organizational investment or safeguards can create risk. Human review remains a qualification on direct reliance on AI outputs; the reported accuracy preferences do not establish actual model performance.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims cover provider firms, corporate and government departments, individual professionals and clients across several professional-service sectors, with distinct adoption and workforce implications.
pts.d: For law and tax/accounting firms, the report associates strategic adoption with improved services, lower costs, revenue opportunities and recruitment advantages. It reports operational developments including new advisory and AI-powered services, changing delivery arrangements and movement away from hourly billing; these developments are situated amid AI and other business pressures rather than attributed exclusively to AI. About one-third of firms are increasing the proportion of work billed other than hourly, while roughly one-quarter of in-house professionals have increased work with firms because of fee arrangements and a similar proportion have dropped a firm over inflexibility. Only around one in ten organizations has begun reducing existing types of roles, including junior intake, moving roles to lower-cost geographies or redefining existing roles. The report therefore does not claim widespread realized junior displacement. Corporate and government in-house departments are distinct buyer-side groups: the Institute says department-specific strategies are associated with more ROI than no strategy or reliance only on an overarching organizational strategy. Corporate legal departments display high investment and usage, whereas government agencies show low levels of both. Professionals are expected to retain domain expertise and higher-order judgment while developing AI skills; those who do not may lose career competitiveness. Team development includes technology/AI, operations, innovation and transformation roles, with differing additional functions for firms and in-house teams. Clients are expected to benefit from faster responses, better experiences and improved value. These enterprise benefits are not presented as evidence of closing unmet civil legal need.
